title: Fewer fires burn along Làrach an Dùin wall
summary: Through a hard winter the coast-people left within the three rings let the farthest fires along the middle wall go dark first, feeding what fuel is left toward those nearest the gate, so that the chain of lights along the rampart burns shorter and thicker each week that passes.

title: The last fire in the rings is let go down
summary: The last of the coast-people still keeping Làrach an Dùin finds every other fire along the wall dark one morning, tends her own alone three days more, then spreads its embers thin across the stone and walks out through the gate and down toward the valleys, carrying nothing from the place she had not carried into it.

title: Làrach an Dùin stands deserted
summary: No fire is lit again along the middle wall of the great fortress, its cistern already fouled past drawing; the gate stands open to every season after, and within a few winters grass finds a footing in the threshold that four hundred pairs of feet had once kept bare.

title: A shepherd finds Làrach an Dùin gate standing open
summary: A shepherd grazing nearer the height than shepherds of that country commonly go finds Làrach an Dùin gate open and unguarded a full year after its last fire, and stands some while at the threshold without going in, an open, unwatched gate proving as sure a stop to him as any raised voice.

title: A grandfather of the western landing will not speak of the height
summary: An old man long settled among shore kin who never went up answers his grandson's question about Làrach an Dùin only with the cold and the wind that found a man through doubled wool, and will say nothing of why he left it or whether he meant, at the time, to come back.

title: A hill trader carries down a woman's words of the height
summary: At a northern landing a hill trader, near enough for once to deal rather than merely watch, understands an old coast-woman to speak of the height she left with neither anger nor relief, touching her own chest as she says it, and carries the plain grief of the gesture home whole.

title: The southern middens grow faster than living memory
summary: As more of the coast-people settle at the shore than the shore has ever held, the middens of the southern landing thicken season on season with the ordinary leavings of a people's swelling numbers, and a landing once counted by the dozen comes to be counted by the score.

title: Three of the coast-people climb to the temple with bars of dark wood
summary: A younger kinsman of the moor's usual watcher sees three coast-people climb the temple's steps in the grey of a morning carrying long bars slung at their backs, tools no outside eye has a name for, carried the plain way a man carries a thing he means to use.

title: The altar's top stone is prised free
summary: Working the better part of a morning with their bars set into some gap the distant watcher cannot make out, the three coast-people lift the altar's top stone whole from the sockets it has held since before any teller's grandfather's grandfather first climbed the steps.

title: The altar stone is carried west out of sight
summary: Slung between the three on the same bars that freed it, the altar's stone is carried down the platform's steps and away west across the hillside, out of the watcher's safe distance, and no account ever says where it comes to rest.

title: The temple platform goes untended
summary: No further climb to the temple is ever marked by the moor's watchers; grass thickens between the platform's fitted stones season on season, and the two sockets that held the altar stand open to whatever the sky puts into them.

title: A traveller of the moor finds a cairn below the empty sockets
summary: Climbing the unswept steps alone, a traveller of the northern moor finds a small, carefully fitted cairn of loose stone set just below the altar's empty sockets, built by no hand he can name and for no purpose the finding itself will explain.

title: The hill country settles the telling of the three ruins
summary: With Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, Làrach an Dùin and the temple all stood empty across the same three valleys, the hill country's tellers let the wonder of the coast-people's high places rest at last on the plain fact of their emptiness, and tell it after, when they tell it at all, exactly as they found it.
